author: Giles Richards at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez
description:
• Lando Norris: ‘People are not giving him enough credit’

  • 20-year-old sealed F1 title after finishing third in Mexico

Formula One’s leading drivers have been unstinting in their praise for the new champion, Kimi Antonelli, after the Italian driver took his debut title with third place at the Mexican Grand Prix.

Antonelli became the youngest world champion at 20 years old in Mexico, sharing a podium with race winner Max Verstappen and second-placed Lewis Hamilton. He has taken the title in only his second year in the sport after a remarkable season including nine wins.

Continue reading...
title: ‘He’s done an insane job’: Antonelli’s rivals unite in praise for F1’s youngest champion

author: Giles Richards at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez
description:
• 20-year-old clinches title with four races to go

  • Verstappen wins race ahead of Hamilton

Kimi Antonelli closed out with the cool command of the greats to win the Formula One world championship by taking third place in the Mexican Grand Prix, a race won after no little drama by Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, from the Ferrari of Lewis Hamilton who was left fuming with his teammate Charles Leclerc, who finished fourth.

In taking his debut F1 title for Mercedes, the 20-year-old Antonelli has etched his name into the record books as the youngest driver to claim the sport’s crown and the first Italian to do so since Alberto Ascari won in 1953. It is Mercedes’ first drivers’ championship since Hamilton last won in 2020 and the team’s 10th.

Continue reading...
title: Kimi Antonelli becomes youngest F1 champion with third place in Mexican GP

author: Hannah J Davies
description:
A Derren Brown-style experiment? A Ghostwatch stunt? Wild rumours have swirled around Bradley Walsh’s Million Pound Shot all week. The hoax has finally been revealed – and its message is terrifying

In late October, some canny viewers began to wonder whether there was something strange about Channel 4’s latest gameshow. Bradley Walsh’s Million Pound Shot had been billed as a new big-money contest with a twist, but information about its pilot episode was strangely minimal. Television and radio producer Chuck Thomas wondered on X whether it could be a Derren Brown-style psychological experiment; a Ghostwatch-esque stunt; or even a dark TV comedy in the vein of the genre-bending series Inside No 9. Indeed, the timing – one day after Halloween – also seemed to point viewers towards some kind of parody or one-off drama.

As more information was revealed about the show – including that its players would stake
title: ‘I can’t afford to lose £3,000’: the ‘gameshow’ that made contestants gamble their own money

author: Agencies
description:
• Gardner Minshew’s heroics inspire Arizona

  • Jackson needs surgery on injured thumb

Chad Ryland kicked a winning 42-yard field goal in overtime after missing a PAT that would have won the game with six seconds left in regulation, and the Arizona Cardinals rallied for a wild victory over the Dallas Cowboys on Sunday. The Cardinals beat Dallas for the fifth consecutive time and improved to 5-0 at AT+T Stadium, the home of the Cowboys that opened in 2009.

Continue reading...
title: NFL roundup: Cardinals’ comeback stuns Cowboys; Lamar Jackson’s season could be over

author: Andy Hunter at Anfield
description:
• Manager rues two dismissed penalty claims by referee

  • Iraola complains ‘if you don’t go down, you don’t call it’

Andoni Iraola said he will instruct Liverpool players to go down in the box in future after Alexander Isak was denied a penalty during Arsenal’s first win at Anfield for 14 years.

Liverpool were beaten by Kai Havertz’s early strike after a poor clearance from the goalkeeper ­Alisson but had two penalty claims dismissed by the referee, Andy Madley. The first, a shirt-pull by the Arsenal defender Jurriën Timber on Isak, prevented the ­Sweden international reaching Bradley Barcola’s cross. The second, a hold by Christos ­Tzolis on Cody Gakpo, was reviewed by the video assistant referee, Stuart Attwell, but rejected.
title: ‘We have to tell them to go down’: Iraola responds to Isak penalty denial for Liverpool

author: Andy Hunter at Anfield
description:
Afternoon began with talk of a title bid, but Arsenal looked more and more comfortable as the second half wore on

Andoni Iraola had swatted aside any question that veered in the direction of Liverpool’s title credentials during his press conference on Friday with two simple words. “Too early,” he would respond. The Liverpool head coach was dismissive in terms of the stage of the season but, as Arsenal doggedly demonstrated, too early also applies to the development of his team.

Arsenal cavorted to the sound of fury at Anfield. At the final whistle Mikel Arteta leapt into the arms of the first-team coach Gabriel Heinze as he celebrated the release of his first win at Liverpool as Arsenal manager, his club’s first league victory at Anfield in 14 years and the champions moving three points clear at the top of the table. His players, tireless in the protection of Kai Havertz’s early winner, lined up to accept the acclaim from a jubilant away section. Anger filled the space
title: Liverpool’s work in progress fizzles out in the face of streetwise champions | Andy Hunter

author: Ella Baron
description: Continue reading...
title: Ella Baron on Donald Trump and the US midterms – cartoon

author: Agencies
description:
• Bellingham and Diomandé complete 3-0 win over Racing

  • Lazio top Serie A after fighting back to beat Cagliari

Kylian Mbappé moved on from a tumultuous week by scoring a penalty to help Real Madrid win 3-0 at Racing Santander on Sunday.

The French forward narrowly lost out on the Ballon d’Or to Bayern Munich’s Harry Kane on Monday and then had to apologise after a social media storm following a video in which he joked about the former Chinese leader Mao Zedong.

This story will be updated

Continue reading...
title: European football: Mbappé penalty helps Real Madrid stroll to sixth straight win

author: Guardian Staff
description:
John Holford, Alan Wells, Jol Miskin and Isobel Hunter Readers respond to an editorial that championed the freedom to learn at any age

Your editorial makes a strong case for lifelong adult education (The Guardian view on adult education: learning should be for all ages, 25 October). But like the report by the all party parliamentary group on further education that it refers to, it overlooks one vital dimension: we need adult education to defend democracy.

For most of the last century, adult education’s role in creating democratic civil society was widely accepted, not least by policymakers. The Ministry of Reconstruction
title: This government should rebuild adult education as a democratic bulwark | Letter

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Dr Will Haydock calls for a new govrnment plan with clear priorities, while a reader in Ecuador points to the devastating impact of UK cocaine use there

The reports published as part of your investigation into cocaine lay bare the widespread harms linked to the drug that people are experiencing (Cocaine-linked crimes on the rise in Britain as consumption surges, 25 October; ‘He was like 10 men after taking cocaine‘: how Britain’s drug habit is fuelling domestic abuse, 26 October).

Similar concerns can be identified in relation to other drugs – including alcohol – and the situation could not be more urgent. Deaths related to drug use have been rising for over a decade
title: A new strategy is needed to address the harms related to cocaine and other drugs | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Dr Ahmad Elabbar reflects on what such a decision means for academics who are working on today’s most difficult and urgent topics

UK higher education is in a confusing and fraught enough state without the government banning distinguished authors on our reading lists such as Andreas Malm (Climate academic Andreas Malm barred from entering UK, 30 October).

Last Thursday I gave a lecture on negative emissions and geoengineering, and recommended The Long Heat, which Malm co-authored with Wim Carton, to my students.

Continue reading...
title: The decision to bar Andreas Malm from entering the UK is farcical and chilling | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Meeting the 0.3% floor is a test of whether it is serious about its commitment to international cooperation, says Callum Northcote

That the UK might miss its 0.3% target on international development spending is rubbing salt into an open wound (Report, 26 October). The UK’s development budget, which tackles global challenges and is a lifeline to millions around the world, has been repeatedly cut over the past five years – it’s estimated that 62 million fewer people will be supported by UK aid around the world in 2026-27 compared with 2019.

When the Labour government announced it was cutting aid to 0.3% of gross national income, it committed to ensuring that this would be the floor, with the intention to increase funding a
title: The UK must stick to its spending pledge on international aid | Letter

author: Editorial
description:
The Covid pandemic shed an unforgiving light on health and social care inequalities. The lessons have yet to be absorbed

The fear that so many felt as the death toll rose during the Covid pandemic was magnified for Fiona Walker. “I know from experience they wouldn’t have valued my life,” she says, in a new report on the treatment of people with learning disabilities during the crisis.

The 1.5 million people in the UK with learning disabilities, and their families, had reason for concern. Death rates in England were four to six times higher than average for people with learning disabilities. As is now well established, the pandemic did not create inequalities; it exposed and intensified them. People with learning disa
title: The Guardian view on listening to people with learning disabilities: a matter of life and death | Editorial

author: Kiran Stacey, Lisa O’Carroll and Jessica Elgot
description:
Exclusive: Plan to allow students from bloc pay same fees as Britons contingent on entry to industrial programme, officials say

Ministers are prepared to spend as much as £450m a year to give students from the EU discounted university fees, the Guardian has learned, but only if Brussels allows the UK access to its Made in Europe industrial programme.

The UK government has drawn up plans to allow students arriving from the continent pay the same fees as British students, sources say, and is willing to spend hundreds of millions of pounds compensating universities to do so.

Continue reading...
title: UK willing to spend £450m a year on EU students if it can join Made in Europe scheme

author: Robert Kitson
description:
• Coach says of need to adjust to refereeing interpretations

  • Genge calls timing of ‘hip-drop’ tackle law change ‘beserk’

Steve Borthwick is urging his England players to act smarter and recognise the vital importance of keeping 15 players on the field before a pivotal month for the national team. Borthwick’s side have been shown 14 yellow cards and one red in 2026 to date and, partly as a consequence, have lost five of their past seven Tests.

Borthwick is also concerned that different refereeing interpretations in the domestic Prem are not helping England at international level, with the latest complication being a mid‑season law change preventing so called “hip-drop” tackles. His experienced prop Ellis Genge has called the timing of the alteration “berserk” but also fully accepts England must improve their disciplinary record in their autumn Nations Championship fixtures.
title: Borthwick urges England players to improve discipline at Nations Championship

author: Chris Hippensteel (now)
description:
He had originally canceled the in-person appearances in favor of tele-rallies, only to reverse course

  • Sign up for the Breaking News US email

The Republican congressman Mike Lawler is in danger of losing his seat next week. Again.

In the last two elections, Lawler, 40, has defeated Democratic opponents in New York’s 17th congressional district – one of the closest-run battlegrounds in this year’s midterms – with moderate policies.

Continue reading...
title: Trump to appear at rallies in battlegrounds Iowa and Kansas two days before midterms – live

author: Suzanne Wrack
description:
• Arsenal salvage late 1-1 draw at home against Aston Villa

  • Chasity Grant fired visitors ahead after 25 minutes

One shot, on target and in the back of the net, was all it took for Aston Villa to reopen the wound that Arsenal had been carefully trying to stitch back up.

Despite almost 65% possession, 28 shots to one, and 56 touches in the opposition box to four, Alessia Russo’s 85th-minute goal meant Arsenal were only able to salvage a point against Villa after back-to-back wins in the league and Champions League had appeared to have kickstarted their season.

Continue reading...
title: Russo spares Arsenal blushes but latest setback increases pressure on Slegers

author: Gautam Malkani
description:
A great picture can have an immediate and visceral effect on a viewer, as if bypassing thought. But a huge amount of thinking goes into selecting and sourcing them, and researching their backstories

Can photographs still exert power in an age when millions of pictures are taken and shared every minute, and when a viewer’s first response is to question whether an image is even real?

Every few months, a team of editors on the Guardian’s Saturday magazine puts together a special photography package in print and digital formats. It features photographs that don’t just stop the scroll, they have also prompted the rewriting of history books. They are the kind of images that have changed the world in some way or radically shifted people’s perceptions.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Some photos imprint upon us’: How our Saturday magazine puts together special issues about world-changing photographs

author: Suzanne Wrack
description:
Goals from Khadija Shaw and Lauren Hemp helped Manchester City escape from Bromley with three points after a thrilling encounter with London City Lionesses. It was a statement performance from the home team, despite the defeat delivering a blow to any title ambitions they may have been quietly holding on to prior to kick-off.

The gap between the hosts and the champions is now six points, after Hemp restored City’s lead following Jana Fernández’s equaliser. But the fact London City have even played their way into the conversation about this season’s title contenders in only their second WSL season is hugely impressive.

Continue reading...
title: Hemp strikes back as Manchester City edge out London City Lionesses in thriller

author: Harriet Gibsone
description:
The presenter recalls being a ‘weird little nerd’, almost becoming a scientist – and the most revealing costume she’s worn for work

Born in Reading in 1973, Lucy Worsley is a historian and TV presenter. She ­graduated with a first in history from Oxford, before completing a PhD in art history at the University of Sussex. Worsley spent 21 years as chief curator of Historic Royal Palaces, overseeing the Tower of London, Hampton Court and Kensington Palace, among others. She has p­resented numerous documentary series, including Six Wives, Royal History’s Biggest Fibs and most recently Victorian Murder Club. She lives in London with her husband. Her latest book, Queens and Kings: An Unusually Personal History, is out now.

This is me at the age of four. It was my career ambition to bec
title: Historian Lucy Worsley looks back: ‘The story of my life has been – the bookworm shall go to the ball’

description:
The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical concepts

This week’s question: if I get a dumbphone, how will I cope in a smartphone world?

As I was building pyramids of loo roll and tinned beans in response to the government’s Be Ready campaign, launched this week, I got to thinking about what other aspects of modern life might help us to get through an emergency. Specifically, our extensive back catalogue of disaster movies, TV series and the like. We’ve imagined catastrophes hitting the human race in so many ways, with so many different outcomes. Are there any useful tips we can take from our library
title: Readers reply: with governments asking us to stockpile, can we learn anything from disaster films?

author: Felicity Cloake
description:
Venison casserole is as autumnal as fallen leaves, a glass of red and a fire in the grate. But who makes the best version?

Because I don’t eat it very often, I always forget how much I like venison. Or, rather, how much I like it in certain contexts: the natural leanness of a wild animal doesn’t naturally lend itself to soloing in juicy burgers or sausages, but, when slow-cooked, it’s fabulous – rich in flavour, and soft enough to eat with a spoon, should you so desire. It also tends to be good value both in season and frozen for the rest of the year, and, as red meat goes, a pretty climate-friendly option (though not straightforwardly so, as this piece explains) that pairs beautifully with seasonal spuds and kales, and is even better when made ahead of time and reheated. In fact, it’s the perfect autumn and winter entertaining option, even if the only people you’r
title: How to make the perfect venison casserole – recipe | Felicity Cloake's How to make the perfect …

author: Jason Wilson
description:
One man’s campaign finance operation in Wisconsin exemplifies the opacity of the US political funding system

In the summer of 2024, a non-profit called the Green Dragon Coalition wired the last $20,000 of a $445,000 grant to a Super Pac. Its tax return for that year would describe the purpose of the transfer as “educational”.

The same day, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) records, the Super Pac spent $8,000 attacking Celeste Maloy, the Republican congresswoman for Utah’s second district, four days before the primary that would decide whether she kept her seat. It had already spent more than $400,000 promoting her challenger, Colby Jenkins, who was running to her right with the endorsement of the rightwing Utah senator Mike Lee.

Continue reading
title: ‘Dark money made darker’: funding labyrinth conceals donors to Republican campaigns

author: Stephen Starr in Springfield, Ohio
description:
Haitian community in Springfield demands dignity and better rights for immigrants as ICE crackdown ramps up

Michaelle Louis’s feet and legs are aching. She can barely walk.

Surrounded by corn fields and the distant hum of a busy highway, the native of Haiti and dozens of other activists are 23 miles into a 45-mile march from Springfield to Ohio’s statehouse in Columbus to demand better rights for Haitian immigrants.

Continue reading...
title: ‘We spend our days in silence’: fear and repression in Ohio as ICE terrorizes Haitian immigrants

author: Jess Cartner-Morley
description:
Whether it’s a two-in-one coat or a truly delicious handbag, add some fun to getting dressed during the cold, dark months with our expert’s favourites

• The best women’s shoes and boots for autumn

The clocks have gone back. The mornings are cold and the evenings are dark. The world seems to be doing its level best to discourage any fashion ambition beyond the need to stay alive and warm enough to function.

But clothes – even in winter – are not just about staying alive. They are about staying alive alive. Alive inside. So this month’s edit is about finding the fun in getting dressed when the weather is trying to discourage you. There is a pink jumper that manages to be both cosy and, well, slutty; a £16 henley that looks considerably more expensive than it is; and a skirt I have been stalking since the summer and can finally report bac
title: Jess Cartner-Morley’s November style essentials: fancy flats, sexy knits and a Christmassy pigeon

author: Sarah Butler
description:
In the final article in a series on high-end British manufacturing we look at a clothing brand that dates to the 18th century but is increasingly on-trend

  • Making jeans again: the Hiut Denim factory in Cardigan

  • Rolls-Royce rides high on craze for customisation

  • Luxury leather: from wallets to cigar cases

Tina is wielding a large pair of scissors with authority, slicing with immense skill and precision.

With 38 years of experience, she is an important member of the 230-strong manufacturing team producing fine knitwear for the John Smedley brand. Using a chalk, a semi-circular guide and a sharp pair of sciss
title: Fashion and tradition: how John Smedley is innovating in a tough market

author: Luke McLaughlin
description:
⚽️ WSL updates with games at 12pm, 2pm and 2.30pm (GMT)
⚽️ Putellas provides mindset change | Mail Luke

As Martin Semmens, the London City Lionesses chief executive, sits down is his office he looks like the cat that got the cream. He says he has just learned that the club’s Instagram page has generated 34m hits since Alexia Putellas won the Ballon d’Or on Monday evening, and it is only Thursday afternoon. On Sunday two clubs with seven of the top 30 players in the Ballon d’Or rankings will go head-to-head when Manchester City visit Hayes Lane, Bromley. It is, Semmens, says, “awesome for the WSL”.

From the outside,
title: Arsenal v Aston Villa, London City Lionesses v Manchester City, and more: Women’s Super League – live

author: Heather Stewart
description:
The Preventative Departmental Expenditure Limit will be money ringfenced in the budget for preventive policies

John Healey’s debut budget was far from a blockbuster, but it may come to be remembered for the birth of a plucky new character in the tax and spend universe – little PDEL.

It may not have the charm of Disney’s Wall-E, but PDEL (pronounced P-Del), Preventative Departmental Expenditure Limit, to give it its full name, marks a welcome, and potentially very consequential, addition.

Continue reading...
title: New public spending category PDEL is a welcome and could have big impact | Heather Stewart

author: Press Association
description:
• Briton beats 18-year-old Austrian Lilli Tagger 4-6, 6-3, 6-4

  • Dart, a qualifier, was competing in her first WTA final

Britain’s Harriet Dart won her first WTA title after coming from a set down to beat Lilli Tagger in the final of the Guangzhou Open in China. Dart, who saved three match points in her semi-final win over Sun Xinran to reach her first tour-level final, edged a thrilling match against the 18-year-old from Austria 4-6, 6-3, 6-4.

Dart, the British No 5 and a qualifier, dropped serve in the opening game and had to save a break point in her next service game before finally getting on the board against the fourth seed. The 30-year-old from Hampstead broke back for 4-4, but Tagger hit straight back before wrapping up the first set.

Continue reading...
title: GB’s Harriet Dart wins maiden WTA title at 30 with Guangzhou Open triumph

author: Flora Willson
description:
Coliseum, London
A sumptuous score and magnificent singing bring real theatrical electricity, even if the relentless violence and radical reimagining don’t always convince

Four years since English National Opera unveiled its previous Tosca (a hyper-stylised affair directed by Christof Loy), the curtain goes up on another new production, this time by ENO’s artistic director Annilese Miskimmon. The appeal of Puccini’s work to any company – never mind one urgently committed to stabilising itself – is clear. Tosca is one of opera’s most bankable titles and a c
title: Tosca review – Axelle Fanyo and Christopher Purves shine in ENO’s reimagined Puccini

author: Bethan McKernan Wales correspondent
description:
Natural Resources Wales says short-necked oil beetle has been found in country for first time in nearly 60 years

A rare beetle has been rediscovered in Wales after nearly 60 years, conservationists have said.

The short-necked oil beetle, driven to the brink of extinction in Britain due to habitat loss over the course of the 20th century, has been found at Castlemartin range in Pembrokeshire, according to Natural Resources Wales (NRW).

Continue reading...
title: Rare beetle that oozes substance from its knees when attacked rediscovered in Wales

author: Tim Jonze
description:
As deadpan spoof documentarian Philomena Cunk returns with a new series on cinema, her creators discuss meeting J-Lo, their worst ever jobs – and why artificial intelligence is like mad cow disease

She has tackled Britain, conquered the world and even grappled with life itself. Now Philomena Cunk is back on our screens – looking as miserable and confused as ever – to take on her biggest subject yet: cinema.

Cinema, the iconically stupid presenter explains, is not just mankind’s greatest achievement but also a world where “men can be heroes, women can get off with heroes, and nobody ever goes to the toilet – unless you’re watching a specialist film from Japan”. So if you’ve ever wanted to know why “Citizen Ken” always has carrots in his pockets, where the word auteur comes from (“They felt they oughta get all the credit”) or how Benedict Cumberbatch reacts to the hardest-hitting questions of his career (such as “Who are you?”), this is quite literally the only p
title: ‘Let’s take Alexa out into the garden and smash it with a shoe’: Charlie Brooker and Diane Morgan take aim at Hollywood, AI ... and each other

author: As told to Rich Pelley
description:
Rapper Pos of the hip hop greats favours Barry White for the bedroom and sobs to Stevie Wonder, but which cheese-rock hit does he love on the sly?

The first song I fell in love with
My father could sing really well – he was in a choir and had this coolness. He would walk around singing Love and Happiness by Al Green and, because he looked so much like him on the cover, I actually thought he was Al Green.

The first single I bought
Underlove by Melba Moore from Abraham & Straus, this department store in Long Island that had a mini record store inside. I later realised it was produced by Kashif, and I would fall in love with everything he produced.

Continue reading...
title: ‘It seems weird for an MC – but lyrics have never been a thing for me’: De La Soul’s honest playlist

author: Rory Scothorne
description:
The PM’s goals may spell bad news for the SNP. Ironically, his EU bridge-building could also resurrect their dreams of independence

Fifty years ago this month, a group of leftwing Scots gathered in the Golden Lion hotel in Stirling for the inaugural conference of a new political party. The “Scottish Labour party” had formally split from Labour at the beginning of 1976, driven by disillusionment over the party’s timid proposals for a new Scottish assembly. They were led by the firebrand MP for South Ayrshire, Jim Sillars, who promised to take Scotland’s Labour tradition back to its roots in both socialism and home rule.

Sillars’ new party was a media sensation in Scotland, and quickly joined by public intellectuals such as Tom Nairn, Hamish Henderson and
title: Why Scottish nationalists should see Burnham as a real threat – and an opportunity | Rory Scothorne

author: Will Unwin at the AIG Stadium
description:
The aim of reaching the Championship looks more realistic for a Manchester club in the shadow of City and United

After seven seasons in League Two, Salford City are finally threatening to match the hype brought by their high-profile owners. First it was the Class of ‘92 who guided them up through the non-league system into the fourth tier but failed to progress any further. Gary Neville and David Beckham remain, part of a new group that took over in May 2025, with this year beginning to look transformational after securing an eighth straight win, against Exeter, to put them five points clear at the top.

The budget has increased, allowing the club to sign a number of players who will feel they are above League Two standard. Striker Macaulay Langstaff arrived from Millwall; the last time he played at this level, he scored 28 goals in a season for Notts County. Matchwinner Will Aimson spent the past two seasons in the division above with Wigan and has dropped down because
title: Rampant Salford hint that Beckham’s lofty ambitions are not a pipe dream

author: Phil Harrison, Jack Seale and Hollie Richardson
description:
Take the plunge with shrimps, starfish and tawny nurse sharks. Plus, a mysterious, gambling-themed “quiz event” with Bradley Walsh. Here’s what to watch this evening

8pm, BBC One
Life is every bit as strange and beautiful at the bottom of the ocean as it is on land – and it is even more profuse. In his 101st year, David Attenborough is still finding amazing things to show us. The quality of footage the BBC Natural History Unit now records is truly startling. The return of this beloved series begins in tropical seas where constant sunlight stimulates an extraordinary range of life. Look out for the remarkable team-hunting strategies of the tawny nurse sharks, as well as an incredible tussle between a pair of shrimps and a starfish that culminates in the shrimp stealing and eating the starfish’s arm (don’t worry, it grows back). Consistently amazing. Phil Harrison
title: TV tonight: oceanic wonder with David Attenborough in Blue Planet III

author: Grace Dent
description:
The crumpet has the texture of a damp Always Ultra

I’ve done some fairly rash things in my time, but I’ve never popped into anywhere for king scallops with ’nduja and come out with a swallow tattoo on my neck, though what is this life without adventure? Which is where Moods comes in: the space is an all-day restaurant, bar, tattoo parlour and hair salon in Leeds, offering violetta potato with ox cheek, a short back and sides, and the chance to tattoo “Mum” on your lower left arm, all in one Grade II-listed building.

It occupies the former First White Cloth Hall on Kirkgate, built in 1711 for the trade of white undyed cloth. This cavernous ark, with roof timbers dating back to the 1470s, lurked on Historic England’s Heritage at Risk register for more than 20 years, during which time it was under almost constant threat from the bulldozers. It took
title: Moods, Leeds LS2: ‘Puzzling, if not quite a car crash’ – restaurant review

author: Annalisa Barbieri
description:
Getting older and losing your autonomy is even harder without family around. You need to consider both the practical and emotional issues involved

My wife and I are in our late 70s, and have been married for more than 40 years. We didn’t have kids and were rather traumatised after failed IVF.

My wife is Asian and has no UK-based family. I do, but they are not close geographically, nor are they people who would be able to give any support if needed. Friends are of a similar age and so have their own issues to deal with. My wife and I have always been a self-reliant unit, and we’re both reasonably healthy, but I’m increasingly aware that there will soon come a time when help is needed.
title: My wife and I are in our late 70s and don’t have any children. Who can help us in our old age? | Annalisa Barbieri

author: Imogen West-Knights
description:
It was so refreshing to hear Aaron Sorkin admit he was bad at parts of directing after his movie flop. If only others could be as frank

By most accounts, Aaron Sorkin’s new film The Social Reckoning, a follow-up to his 2010 smash-hit The Social Network, is a flop. The film critic Mark Kermode’s response to seeing it was that Sorkin, who is widely regarded as one of the greatest living screenwriters, is “not a great director”.

It seems that Sorkin agrees. Because Sorkin is very famous, he has had to do the rounds talking about the film in the media, which led to his appearance on the Hollywood Reporter’s
title: I’m sick of smug celebrities on the podcast circuit. No wonder there’s a fuss when someone speaks the truth | Imogen West-Knights

author: William Christou and Sufian Taha in Um Rukbeh
description:
Kinaan Dadou, 10, has been left disabled since 7 October 2023 as his parents struggle to find funding for specialist treatment

It was 7.30am on 7 October 2023 when a Hamas rocket exploded next to 7-year-old Kinaan Dadou. The rocket was aimed at the Israeli settlement of Efrat in the occupied West Bank but missed its mark by a few hundred metres, landing in front of Kinaan’s family home instead.

A piece of shrapnel struck Kinaan in the head. He stood rigid, his hands frozen to his sides, and screamed “Baba!” before collapsing to the ground. An Israeli soldier who passed by promised to call an ambulance. No help ever came. Kinaan’s parents rushed him to the hospital themselves, but it was six hours before a doctor arrived due to the chaos of the day. All the while, Kinaan’s brain was haemorrhaging.

Continue reading...
title: ‘What’s our crime?’: A Palestinian family’s fight to get care for son injured by Hamas rocket

author: Chris Wiegand
description:
An unmissable documentary play, Tom Stoppard’s Arcadia with luminous Isis Hainsworth and ecstatic dance in a Norwegian museum are among November’s highlights

Swiss director Milo Rau’s ripped-from-the-headlines approach to theatre has included shows about wars in Iraq and Congo and the exploitation of migrant workers. His four-hour documentary play (created with Servane Dècle) about the trial of the men who drugged and raped Gisèle Pelicot has been performed around the world and will be staged by the Young Vic at London’s County Hall on 30 November. The production swiftly sold out but will be livestreamed in full.
